title: Risks and Responsible Use
summary: Students meet the two basic risk families of AI use - accuracy and safety/privacy - name who each risk could affect, and agree responsible-use rules that reduce them.
objectives: Identify at least two basic risks of using AI tools (e.g., incorrect output, unsafe or private data use).
Explain why each risk matters and who it could affect.
State one responsible-use rule that reduces a risk.

sections.heading: Risks and Responsible Use
body: An AI answer can look helpful and still put someone at risk - through a mistake you did not check, or through personal data you should never have shared.
Today you learn to spot those risks and to name the rule that keeps people safe.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can name two genuine risks of using an AI tool.
I can explain who each risk could affect.
I can state a responsible-use rule that reduces a risk.

terms.definition: Something that could go wrong when using a tool.
The danger of acting on an incorrect output.
Keeping personal or identifying information safe and unshared.
Information that identifies a person, like a name, address, or photo.
An agreed habit that reduces a risk.

sections.heading: Two risk families
body: **Accuracy risk** is the danger of using a confident but incorrect output without checking it. The mistake can spread into your work and anyone who trusts it.
**Safety and privacy risk** is the danger of entering [[personal data]] or identifying data, which may be stored or used to train future systems and could expose you or someone else.

sections.label: Two families, different responses
sections.heading: What kind of risk is this?
sections.altText: A risk splits into two families: the output being wrong, and the tool being used unsafely. Each has a different response.

branches.label: The output is wrong
branches.detail: → check it before anyone acts on it

branches.label: The use is unsafe
branches.detail: → change what goes in, or do not use it

sections.caption: Naming the family tells you the response. **Checking harder does not fix a privacy problem**, and removing personal details does not make a wrong fact right.

sections.heading: Every risk has a who
body: A real risk always names who could be harmed - you, a classmate, or your family.
[[Responsible-use rule]]s are simple habits, agreed together, that reduce a risk: verify before you use, never enter personal data, and tell an adult if you are unsure.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Sort each scenario into a risk family, name who is affected, and choose a responsible-use rule that would reduce the risk.
items: Decide: accuracy risk or safety/privacy risk.
Attach a responsible-use rule that reduces the risk.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which risk do you think is easiest to forget about, and why?
Is a rule useful if it is too hard to follow?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write one responsible-use rule you will follow from now on.
Describe a situation where you would refuse to enter data into a tool.

worksheet.title: Week 5 - Core - Worksheet | Risks and Responsible Use

questions.prompt: Layla asks an AI tool what time the school science fair opens. She copies the answer straight onto a poster that goes up in the main corridor. Which risk family is this, and who could it affect?

options.text: Accuracy risk - if the time is wrong, everyone who reads the poster could arrive at the wrong time.
Accuracy risk - but only Layla is affected, because it is her poster.
Safety and privacy risk - the AI tool now knows when the science fair is.
Safety and privacy risk - Layla typed a question into a tool that may store what she asks.

feedback.correct: Exactly - an unchecked output is an accuracy risk, and the harm spreads to everyone who trusts the work it goes into.
feedback.incorrect: No personal data was entered here, so this is an accuracy risk - and a wrong time on a public poster reaches far more people than just Layla.

questions.prompt: Ravi wants an AI tool to tidy up the wording of a party invitation. Before he types his draft into the tool, which details should he take out?

options.text: His classmate Sara Ahmed's full name
His home address, Villa 12, Al Rayyan Street
The fact that the party starts at four o'clock
The fact that there will be pizza and a cake

feedback.correct: Right - names, addresses and phone numbers identify real people, so they are the parts that create a privacy risk if the tool stores them.
feedback.incorrect: The risk is in details that identify a person - a full name, an address, a phone number. A start time and a menu identify nobody.

questions.prompt: Match each situation to the responsible-use rule that would reduce its risk.

left.text: Omar pastes an AI answer about how volcanoes form straight into his science report.
Mei types a classmate's full name and home address into a chatbot so it can write a thank-you note.
Yusuf finds a new AI app online and is not sure whether it is safe to use for homework.

right.text: Never enter personal or identifying data into an AI tool.
Tell an adult if you are unsure about a tool.
Check the output against a trusted source before you use it.

feedback.correct: Good matching - a rule only counts as useful when it actually reduces the particular risk in front of you.
feedback.incorrect: Ask what could go wrong in each case: a wrong fact needs checking, identifying details should never be typed in, and an unknown tool needs an adult.

questions.prompt: Put the four steps of the risk-check routine into the order the lesson uses them.

items.text: Attach a responsible-use rule that reduces the risk.
Decide whether it is an accuracy risk or a safety and privacy risk.

feedback.correct: That is the chain - risk, then who, then rule. The rule comes last because it has to fit the risk you named.
feedback.incorrect: You cannot pick a rule until you know what the risk is and who it could harm, so the rule is always the last step.

questions.prompt: True or false: a mistake in an AI answer only affects the person who asked the question.

feedback.correct: Correct - an unchecked mistake spreads into your work and on to anyone who trusts it, which is why every risk has a who.
feedback.incorrect: Think about where the answer ends up: in a report, a poster or a message, so the mistake reaches everyone who trusts that work.

formative.targets: Directly checks 'recognises basic risks (incorrect outputs, unsafe use)'
formative.check: Risk-spotting exit card: name two risks + one responsible-use rule
formative.successCriteria: Names two genuine risks, explains who is affected, and states a matching responsible-use rule.
